239.title: Buddhism: the man under the tree
239.hook: Siddhartha leaves a palace, sits under a tree at Bodh Gaya, and wakes up
239.howItsDone: Buddhists around the world tell the story of the Buddha's leaving home and awakening, and many make pilgrimage to Bodh Gaya, where a descendant of the Bodhi tree still grows beside the Mahabodhi Temple.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diwali, the row of lamps that closed our Hindu visit. Your line was light over dark. Whose dark did you bring a little light to? Day two hundred thirty-nine, and a new visit: Buddhism.

Imagine being given everything. A palace, a beautiful family, servants, music, a future as king, and a father determined that you'll never see anything sad. Then, one day, you see it anyway. Old age. Sickness. A body being carried to be burned. And a wandering holy man, calm in the middle of it all. You can't unsee it. That, in the story Buddhists tell, is how a young prince named Siddhartha Gautama walked out of his palace one night and went looking for a way through. Today we visit Buddhism.
screen: `GIVEN EVERYTHING.` → `OLD AGE, SICKNESS, DEATH, A MONK.` → `THE PRINCE WALKS OUT.`

segments.voice: Siddhartha was born in Lumbini, in what's now southern Nepal, into the Shakya clan, probably in the fifth century before Christ; scholars still debate the exact dates. The story of the four sights, the old man, the sick man, the corpse and the monk, comes from later biographies, and Buddhists treasure it as the heart of why he left. He left at twenty-nine. For about six years he tried everything the holy men of his day taught, including fasting so hard, the texts say, that he could feel his spine through his stomach. It didn't work. So he did something his companions thought was giving up: he ate. A bowl of rice and milk, offered, in the traditional story, by a young woman named Sujata. Then he sat down under a tree at a place now called Bodh Gaya, in northern India, and resolved not to get up until he understood. The tradition says Mara, the tempter, came with fear and desire and doubt, and that Siddhartha touched the earth as his witness. Through the night he saw clearly, and by dawn, Buddhists say, he had woken up. That's the name: Buddha comes from a root meaning to wake. The Buddha is the awakened one. The tree became the Bodhi tree, the tree of awakening. Buddhists across many schools honor him not as a creator god but as a teacher who found the way and showed it. The texts even say that at first he hesitated to teach, thinking no one would understand. Then he got up and walked to find his old companions.
screen: `A PRINCE BORN IN LUMBINI.` · `SIX YEARS OF STARVING: NO.` · `A BOWL OF RICE, THEN THE TREE.` · `BUDDHA: THE AWAKENED ONE.` · then, large: `WAKE UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit under a tree, or picture one. If you're near a tree, go and sit with your back to it. If not, picture a wide, shady tree above you, its leaves moving. Settle and breathe. Let your hand rest on the ground, or on the floor, or your knee: something solid. Just be awake to what's here. The sounds. The air. Your breathing. Nothing to become. Just awake. The bell holds the time.
Buddhism. The path of the Buddha, the awakened one: a prince who left his palace, sat under a tree at Bodh Gaya, and woke up. Today's word.
Your line: wake up. Today, three times, stop wherever you are and notice one thing you'd been sleepwalking past: a face, a sound, the sky. Day two hundred thirty-nine.

240.title: Buddhism: the first truth
240.hook: life is marked by unsatisfactoriness, and there is a way through (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)
240.howItsDone: Buddhists of every school study the four noble truths as the foundation of the teaching; many Theravada Buddhists chant the first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, on special days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prince under the tree who woke up. Your line was wake up. What did you notice that you'd been sleepwalking past? Day two hundred forty.

You finally get the thing. The phone, the job, the apartment, the relationship status. And for about a week it's wonderful. Then something is slightly off. The phone is already old. The job has a boss. The apartment has a neighbor with a drum kit. It isn't a tragedy. It's just that faint, familiar sense that things never quite land. After the Buddha woke up, he walked to a deer park and gave his first teaching. And the very first thing he named was that feeling. Today's word: dukkha.
screen: `YOU FINALLY GET THE THING.` → `SOMETHING IS SLIGHTLY OFF.` → `DUKKHA.`

segments.voice: The Buddha's first teaching was given at the Deer Park near Varanasi, to the five companions who had once fasted with him. Buddhists call it the setting in motion of the wheel of the teaching, and it's recorded in the Samyutta Nikaya, a collection in the Pali Canon. In it he lays out four noble truths, a bit like a doctor's diagnosis. First, the illness: dukkha. Second, its cause: craving, a thirst that keeps grasping. Third, the good news: it can end. Fourth, the cure: a path, the noble eightfold path. Now, dukkha is often translated suffering, and that's part of it: birth, aging, sickness and death, being stuck with what you don't want, being parted from what you love. But the word is wider than pain. It's also stress, friction, unsatisfactoriness. The sense that even pleasant things can't fully satisfy, because they change and pass. There's a popular explanation that dukkha once described a wheel with a badly fitted axle, so every ride is a little bumpy. Scholars debate that origin, but many teachers use the picture, and it fits the feeling. Here's the part people miss. The first truth isn't the Buddha saying life is miserable, full stop. It's the first of four. A doctor who names your illness isn't being gloomy; he's starting treatment. Buddhists call these truths noble because seeing them clearly is the beginning of freedom. The whole point of naming dukkha is the fourth truth: there's a way through.
screen: `THE DEER PARK, THE FIRST TEACHING.` · `ILLNESS, CAUSE, CURE, PATH.` · `NOT JUST PAIN: UNSATISFACTORINESS.` · `NAMED IN ORDER TO HEAL.` · then, large: `THERE'S A WAY THROUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one dissatisfaction, without the story. Settle and breathe. Let something that's bothering you come up. Maybe small, maybe not. Now try to feel it without the story: not who did what, or why it's unfair. Just the feeling itself. Where is it in your body? Is it tight, heavy, restless? Name it plainly: this is dukkha. Then keep breathing beside it. The bell holds the time.
Dukkha. Pali for suffering, stress, unsatisfactoriness: the first of the Buddha's four noble truths, named so it can be healed. Today's word.
Your line: there's a way through. Today, when something feels slightly off, name it, drop the story for one breath, and remember the first truth isn't the last. Day two hundred forty.

241.title: Buddhism: everything changes
241.howItsDone: Buddhists reflect on anicca in meditation, watching sensations, thoughts and breath arise and pass, and many chant verses on impermanence, especially at funerals and memorials.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dukkha, the first noble truth. Your line was there's a way through. Did you name something without its story? Day two hundred forty-one.

Scroll back through your photos five years. The haircut. The friends you don't see anymore. The apartment. The face, a bit younger. Nothing dramatic happened, and yet almost everything is different. We know this, of course. But we live as if the good things will stay exactly as they are, and the bad things will last forever. Yesterday the Buddha named the unsatisfactoriness of life. Today, one of the main reasons for it, and, surprisingly, one of the main ways through. Today's word: anicca.
screen: `FIVE YEARS OF PHOTOS.` → `THE GOOD WILL STAY, THE BAD WILL LAST.` → `ANICCA.`

segments.voice: Anicca is a Pali word. Nicca means lasting, constant. The a in front means not. So anicca: not lasting, impermanent. Buddhists count it among the three marks of everything that exists, alongside dukkha, which we met yesterday, and a third, not-self, which is a lesson for another day. The Dhammapada, a beloved collection of the Buddha's sayings, puts it in verse two hundred seventy-seven. In Max Müller's 1881 translation it begins: "All created things perish." Everything that's put together, that arises from causes, will come apart. Mountains, bodies, moods, friendships, empires, this breath. The verse goes on: whoever sees this clearly grows weary of suffering, and that is the path to purity. Here's the turn. Impermanence sounds like the bad news, and part of it is. It's why pleasant things never fully satisfy. But look at it the other way. The terrible week will also pass. The anger you feel right now is already changing. The habit you hate is not carved in stone. If everything were permanent, nothing could heal and no one could grow. Impermanence is also what makes the way through possible. Buddhist texts record that as the Buddha lay dying, his last words to his followers returned to this: all things that are put together fall apart, so keep going, with care. Not a sad line. A practical one. So the carry is two small words you can say to anything, good or bad: this too. This too will change.
screen: `NICCA: LASTING. ANICCA: NOT.` · `ALL CREATED THINGS PERISH.` · `THE BAD WEEK PASSES TOO.` · `THE LAST WORDS: KEEP GOING.` · then, large: `THIS TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch something change. Settle and breathe. Your breath is the easiest thing to watch. Notice that no two breaths are the same. One is longer, one catches, one is soft. Then widen out: sounds come and go, an itch arrives and fades, a thought flares and dissolves. Each time you notice something pass, say inside: this too. The bell holds the time.
Anicca. Pali for impermanence: everything put together changes and passes, the good and the bad. Today's word.
Your line: this too. Today, say it once to something good, so you enjoy it fully, and once to something hard, so you can bear it. Day two hundred forty-one.

it's also why the bad week passes and why people can heal and grow.

options: enjoy it fully, because it will pass.
try hard to make it last forever.
fork.reveal: seeing that everything passes is meant to loosen the grip, not spoil the moment. this too, good and bad.

242.title: Buddhism: loving-kindness
242.hook: may all beings be happy and at ease (Sutta Nipata 1.8)
242.howItsDone: Many Buddhists chant the Karaniya Metta Sutta and practice metta meditation, offering goodwill in turn to themselves, a loved one, a neutral person, a difficult person and all beings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, anicca, everything changes. Your line was this too. Did you say it once to something good and once to something hard? Day two hundred forty-two.

Think about the way a mother looks at a newborn asleep. Nothing is being asked of that baby. It hasn't earned anything or done anything useful. And the love is total: she'd step in front of a truck for it. Now imagine feeling even a small slice of that toward the person ahead of you in line. Toward the driver who cut you off. Toward every living creature, seen and unseen. It sounds impossible. The Buddha taught that it can be practiced, a little at a time, like a muscle. Today's word: metta.
screen: `A MOTHER AND A SLEEPING BABY.` → `THE PERSON AHEAD OF YOU IN LINE.` → `METTA.`

segments.voice: Metta is Pali, often translated loving-kindness or goodwill. It's related to the word for a friend, so you could also hear it as friendliness, wishing someone well the way a true friend does. The most famous teaching on it is a short text in the Sutta Nipata, one of the oldest parts of the Pali Canon, called the discourse on loving-kindness. Buddhist tradition tells that it was first given to a group of monks who were frightened while meditating in a forest. The discourse begins with character: be capable, upright, gentle, not proud, content with little. Then it opens out into wishing. May all beings be happy and at ease. And it lists them, so no one is left out: weak or strong, tall or short, large or small, seen or unseen, near or far, those already born and those yet to be born. May all beings be happy. Then comes the picture from our hook. Just as a mother would protect her only child with her own life, so let a person cultivate a boundless heart toward all beings. Many Buddhists across schools practice metta in meditation, often in a traditional order. First toward yourself. Then someone you love. Then someone you feel neutral about. Then someone difficult. And finally, outward, to all beings everywhere. The phrases are simple and often quiet: may you be well, may you be happy, may you be safe. The idea isn't to fake a feeling. It's to keep pointing the heart in a direction, until the direction becomes a habit.
screen: `METTA: GOODWILL, FRIENDLINESS.` · `SEEN OR UNSEEN, NEAR OR FAR.` · `AS A MOTHER GUARDS HER ONLY CHILD.` · `YOU, A FRIEND, A STRANGER, A FOE.` · then, large: `MAY ALL BEINGS BE WELL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wish three people well, the way many Buddhists do. Settle and breathe. First, someone easy to love. Picture them and, inside, offer the traditional wish: may you be well, may you be happy. Then someone neutral, a neighbor, a cashier. The same wish. Then, if you're willing, someone a little difficult. Not the hardest person. Just a little difficult. The same wish. Then let it spread wider. The bell holds the time.
Metta. Pali for loving-kindness, friendliness, goodwill: wishing all beings happiness, as a mother guards her only child. Today's word.
Your line: may all beings be well. Today, three times, silently wish a stranger well: on the street, on a screen, in a car beside you. Day two hundred forty-two.

243.title: Buddhism: the middle way
243.hook: neither indulgence nor harshness, the Buddha's first teaching (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)
243.howItsDone: Buddhists speak of the Buddha's path as the middle way between indulgence and self-mortification, practiced as the noble eightfold path; the story of Sona's lute is often told to people who push themselves too hard.

segments.voice: Yesterday, metta, loving-kindness. Your line was may all beings be well. Did you wish a stranger well three times? Day two hundred forty-three.

January. You're going to change everything. Up at five, cold showers, no sugar, no screens, run every day. By the third week you're exhausted and furious, and by February you're on the couch eating cereal from the box at midnight, feeling like a failure. Then the cycle starts again. Most of us swing between too much and too little. The Buddha knew that swing from the inside. He'd lived both ends of it, the palace and the starving years. So the first thing he taught about the path was where to walk. Today: Buddhism's middle way.
screen: `UP AT FIVE, COLD SHOWERS.` → `CEREAL AT MIDNIGHT.` → `THE SWING, AND THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Remember the Deer Park, and the five companions who had watched Siddhartha starve himself, then walked away in disgust when he ate. When the Buddha came back to them, the Samyutta Nikaya records, the very first thing he said, even before the four noble truths, was about two extremes to avoid. One is chasing sense pleasures: low, he says, and not leading anywhere good. The other is tormenting yourself: painful, and just as useless. He'd tried both. Between them, he said, there's a middle way, which leads to clear seeing, to peace and to awakening. And he names it: the noble eightfold path. Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. The middle isn't lukewarm. It's balance that works. There's a lovely story about this in another collection, the Anguttara Nikaya. A monk named Sona practiced so hard, walking in meditation, that his feet bled, and still he got nowhere. He was ready to quit and go home. The Buddha came to him and asked: before you became a monk, you played the lute, didn't you? When the strings were too tight, did it sound good? No. Too loose? No. And when they were tuned, not too tight, not too loose? Then it sounded just right. Effort is like that, the Buddha told him. Too much makes you restless, too little makes you lazy. Tune it. Sona did, and the texts say he went on to awakening.
screen: `TWO EXTREMES: INDULGE OR TORMENT.` · `BETWEEN THEM, A PATH.` · `THE NOBLE EIGHTFOLD PATH.` · `SONA'S LUTE: TUNE THE STRINGS.` · then, large: `THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the middle in one habit. Settle and breathe. First, tune your sitting. Are you straining, too upright, jaw tight? Loosen a little. Slumping, drifting? Lift a little. Find the tuned string. Then pick one habit you swing on: food, exercise, work, your phone. Picture the too-tight version, and the too-loose one. Now picture the middle, something you could actually keep. The bell holds the time.
Buddhism's middle way. Neither indulgence nor self-torment: the path between them, named in the Buddha's first teaching. Today's word.
Your line: the middle. Today, in the habit you picked, do the tuned version once: not the heroic one, not the collapse, the one you could do every day. Day two hundred forty-three.

244.title: Buddhism: three refuges
244.hook: Buddhists take refuge in the Buddha, the teaching and the community
244.howItsDone: Buddhists of every school recite the three refuges, usually three times over, at the start of practice and at ceremonies; taking refuge formally is how many people become Buddhist.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sona's lute and the middle way. Your line was the middle. Did you do the tuned version of your habit? Day two hundred forty-four.

Where do you go when it rains hard? Not just weather rain. The phone call with bad news, the month that goes sideways. Most of us have a few shelters, even if we've never named them. A person we call first. A place. A book or a song. Buddhists have named theirs, very precisely, for two and a half thousand years. Three shelters, said aloud, often three times over, at the start of practice, at ceremonies, at the moment someone becomes a Buddhist. The third one is today's word: sangha.
screen: `WHERE DO YOU GO WHEN IT RAINS?` → `THREE NAMED SHELTERS.` → `SANGHA.`

segments.voice: The three refuges, sometimes called the three jewels, are the simplest expression of being Buddhist. In Pali they begin: "Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi." I go to the Buddha for refuge. Then the dhamma, the teaching. Then the sangha, the community. Then the whole thing is said a second time, and a third. Saraṇa, refuge, means a shelter, a safe place, somewhere to stand. Buddhists explain it this way. The Buddha is the example: proof, they say, that a human being can wake up. The dhamma is the map: the teaching and the path we've spent this week visiting, the four truths, impermanence, loving-kindness, the middle way. And the sangha is the company for the road. Sangha means a gathering, a community, and here's where Buddhists use it in more than one way. In its traditional sense, sangha means the community of monks and nuns, who keep the teaching alive and are supported by lay Buddhists with food and care. In another sense, it means the noble community, all those who've truly begun to wake up, in any age. And many Buddhists today, especially in the West, use sangha for the whole community of practitioners, lay and monastic. There's a well-known exchange in the Samyutta Nikaya: the Buddha's attendant Ananda says good friendship is half of the holy life, and the Buddha corrects him. Not half, Ananda. The whole of it. A path this long isn't meant to be walked alone.
screen: `BUDDHA, DHAMMA, SANGHA.` · `SARANA: A SHELTER.` · `EXAMPLE, MAP, COMPANY.` · `NOT HALF: THE WHOLE OF IT.` · then, large: `THREE REFUGES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name what shelters you. Settle and breathe. Ask yourself three quiet questions, borrowing the Buddhist shape without borrowing their vow. Who shows me that a better way is possible? What teaching, or words, do I come back to when it's hard? Who walks with me? Let a face, a line, a group come for each. Just notice them. Be grateful if gratitude comes. The bell holds the time.
Sangha. Pali for community: the third of Buddhism's three refuges, after the Buddha and the teaching. Today's word.
Your line: three refuges. Today, contact one person from your answer to the third question, who walks with me, and thank them for the company. Day two hundred forty-four.

245.title: Vesak, the full moon
245.hook: many Buddhists mark the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing on the full moon of Vesakha
245.howItsDone: On Vesak many Buddhists visit temples, offer flowers and lamps, keep extra precepts, listen to teachings and give food and help; in Sri Lanka streets fill with lanterns and free food stalls called dansal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Buddha, the teaching and the sangha. Your line was three refuges. Who did you thank for walking with you? Day two hundred forty-five, the last day of our Buddhist visit.

Picture a night in Colombo, in Sri Lanka, in late spring. Every street hung with paper lanterns, some as big as houses, lit from inside. Free food stalls handing out rice and tea to anyone passing, no money asked. White-clad families walking to the temple with flowers and oil lamps. And overhead, a full moon. Across Asia and far beyond, many Buddhists keep this one night as the most important of their year. Today we close our visit with it. Vesak, the full moon.
screen: `LANTERNS AS BIG AS HOUSES.` → `FREE FOOD, NO MONEY ASKED.` → `VESAK, THE FULL MOON.`

segments.voice: Vesak takes its name from Vesakha, a month in the old Indian calendar, and the festival falls on its full moon, usually in April or May. In the Theravada tradition, followed in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos, Buddhists hold that three great events in the Buddha's life all happened on that same full moon. His birth in Lumbini. His awakening under the tree at Bodh Gaya. And, eighty years after his birth, his passing into final nirvana at Kushinagar. One night for a whole life. Other Buddhist traditions keep the calendar differently. In much of East Asia, the Buddha's birthday is its own festival, and in Japan his awakening is often marked separately, in December. In Tibet, a whole holy month, Saga Dawa, marks these events. So once again, who you ask matters. What people do on Vesak is quieter than you'd think for such a big night. They visit the temple, offer flowers, light lamps and incense. Many keep extra precepts for the day, eating simply and avoiding harm. And they give: food, lanterns, help. In East Asia children pour scented water over a small statue of the baby Buddha. In 1999 the United Nations recognized the Day of Vesak internationally. And that closes our week with Buddhists. The man under the tree who woke up. Dukkha, and the way through. Anicca, this too. Metta, may all beings be well. The middle way and Sona's lute. The three refuges. And a full moon to hold them all.
screen: `VESAKHA: THE MONTH'S FULL MOON.` · `BIRTH, AWAKENING, PASSING.` · `EACH TRADITION'S OWN CALENDAR.` · `FLOWERS, LAMPS, GIVING.` · then, large: `THE FULL MOON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the moon, or picture it full. If the moon is up and you can see it, go and look. If not, picture a full moon rising over a temple roof, round and white. Settle and breathe. Let one thing from this week come back to you: waking up, the way through, this too, goodwill, the middle, the three shelters. Let the moon hold it. The bell holds the time.
Vesak. The full moon of Vesakha, when many Buddhists mark the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing, with lamps, flowers and giving. Today's word.
Your line: the full moon. Look up tonight and find the moon, whatever its shape. Then give one thing away freely, the way Vesak's food stalls do. Day two hundred forty-five.

many Theravada Buddhists do; in much of East Asia, the birthday and awakening are kept separately.
Vesak falls on a full moon, usually in April or May
the full moon of the month of Vesakha.
Vesak is mostly fireworks and feasting
it's temple visits, flowers, lamps, extra precepts and giving.

fork.setup: it's Vesak night in Colombo. you've set up a stall on your street. what do you do with the food?
options: give it away to anyone passing.
fork.reveal: on Vesak many Sri Lankans run dansal, free food stalls, giving to anyone who passes. giving is one of the heart practices of the night.

original.note: Pali: Vesakha, the month whose full moon is Vesak.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddha's birthday.
what it means: for many Buddhists, one full moon marking birth, awakening and final passing.
what a scholar hears: the triple commemoration is Theravada; the World Fellowship of Buddhists endorsed it in 1950, and the UN recognized the Day of Vesak in 1999.

sources.ref: Buddhist festival calendar (Vesak, Visakha Puja, Saga Dawa)
